title: Passage Triage for a Records Backlog
summary: A batch service that reads a decade of scanned records, splits them into passages, and routes each one to the team that owns it, with the uncertain cases sent to a person instead of guessed.
role: Sole engineer, from ingestion through the review queue
team: Solo, alongside two records officers who defined the routing rules

cover.alt: Placeholder standing in for the passage triage project cover image.

overview: The backlog was a decade of scanned correspondence that nobody could search and everybody needed. The job was not classification accuracy in the abstract. It was deciding, for each passage, which of eleven teams would have to act on it, and being honest about the passages where the answer was not clear.

Everything runs as a batch. Embeddings are stored beside the passages in one database rather than in a separate index, because a second store would have meant a second thing to keep in step with a corpus that changes weekly, and the corpus was never large enough for that trade to pay.
capabilities: Splits scanned records into passages that keep their page and document provenance
Embeds and stores every passage beside its source row rather than in a separate index
Routes each passage to one of eleven owning teams by nearest labelled neighbours
Sends low-confidence passages to a human review queue instead of guessing
Feeds every reviewed decision back in as a labelled example on the next run
Reports what changed between runs so a routing shift is noticed rather than discovered

features.title: Uncertainty is a routing destination
features.body: Passages that do not clear the margin between the top two teams go to a review queue rather than to whichever team scored highest. A confident wrong routing costs a person a week of chasing; an explicit unknown costs them a minute.

features.title: One store for text and vectors
features.body: The embeddings live in the same table as the passages. Two stores would have needed a reconciliation job, a second backup, and an answer for what happens when they disagree, all bought against a corpus small enough that one index was never the bottleneck.

features.title: Review decisions are training data
features.body: Every queue decision is written back as a labelled example, so the next run has more to work with than the last. The label store is append-only, which means a bad batch of labels can be excluded by date rather than untangled row by row.

features.title: Run-to-run diffing
features.body: Each run reports which passages changed team since the previous one. That is the signal that catches a drifting embedding model or a mislabelled batch, and it is cheap because both runs are already in the database.

codeSnippets.title: Passages and their vectors in one table
codeSnippets.code:
CREATE TABLE passage (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  document_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES document (id),
  page         int  NOT NULL,
  ordinal      int  NOT NULL,
  body         text NOT NULL,
  embedding    vector(768),
  routed_team  text,
  routed_at    timestamptz
);

-- Provenance is a uniqueness constraint, not a convention: two passages claiming the
-- same page and ordinal means the splitter ran twice on one document.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX passage_provenance ON passage (document_id, page, ordinal);

CREATE INDEX passage_embedding ON passage USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

lessons: An explicit unknown is a feature with its own interface, not a null that fell out of a threshold.
A second index is not free. It is a reconciliation job, a backup, and an answer for the day the two stores disagree.
Diffing consecutive runs found more real problems than any single-run accuracy number did.
